title: Trump Rolls Back Fuel Economy Standards as Gas Prices Rise
summary:
The Trump administration is rolling back federal fuel economy standards for new vehicles, a move that reverses Biden-era policies designed to push automakers toward building more electric vehicles. The new rule sets the fleet-wide average at 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031. Under the old rules, that average would have been over 50 mpg.

The change gives automakers more flexibility over how fuel-efficient their cars and trucks must be. It also relaxes requirements for controlling pollution. According to the administration, the shift will reduce the cost of a new vehicle by about $1,300. David Shepardson, a transportation reporter for Reuters, said companies like GM could see a $20 billion reduction in estimated costs between now and 2031.

But Shepardson noted there is no guarantee automakers will pass those savings on to buyers. He also pointed out that fuel costs over the life of a vehicle would increase by about $1,600 on average — meaning drivers could actually pay more overall than they save upfront.

The move comes as the war in Iran continues to drive up oil prices. It is part of a broader strategy to make gas-powered vehicles easier to buy and to de-emphasize electric vehicles. A $7,500 EV tax credit has already ended, and the new rules remove regulatory credits that previously rewarded automakers for building EVs.

Transportation Secretary Duffy said the change will let automakers "make vehicles American people want to buy, not what Washington is forcing them to build." Automakers disliked the Biden rules, which they said amounted to an EV mandate. The administration agrees, though the Biden administration had not required all vehicles to be electric.

What happens next to the EV market is uncertain. Shepardson said a lot depends on the 2028 elections. One exception remains: California still has the right to regulate vehicles and require electric cars, though Republicans in Congress are trying to revoke that authority.
why_it_matters: Fuel economy rules decide what kinds of cars get built for the next decade, so a change now shapes what sits on dealership lots — and what families pay at the pump — long after today's politicians leave office. It is also a live example of how policy can swing sharply every few years, forcing whole industries to plan around politics instead of a stable target.

background_read: The rules being rolled back are the U.S. government's fuel economy standards, often called CAFE (Corporate Average Fuel Economy), created in the 1970s after the oil crisis to make cars burn less gasoline. Each new administration sets its own target, so the numbers have swung up and down as power changed hands — which is why carmakers complain they must plan years ahead around rules that keep being rewritten.

The 'Biden-era' rules refer to President Joe Biden (U.S. president from 2021 to 2025), whose administration pushed stricter targets and bigger incentives for electric cars. President Donald Trump's administration (in office since January 2025) argues those rules effectively told companies what to build.

General Motors, or GM, is one of America's largest carmakers and a major maker of pickup trucks and SUVs, so looser standards matter a lot to its costs. Reuters is a large international news agency, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy heads the U.S. Department of Transportation, the agency that sets these vehicle rules.

One legal quirk: under the Clean Air Act, California — the biggest U.S. car market — has long held a special waiver letting it set its own, stricter vehicle pollution rules, and other states can follow it. That is why the fight over these standards is partly a fight over California's authority.

perspectives.description: Companies like GM gain flexibility and lower projected costs — the article cites a $20 billion reduction through 2031 — and people who want large gas-powered trucks should find them cheaper and easier to buy. The administration frames this as giving people what they actually want, rather than what regulators in Washington prefer.

Critics argue the rollback slows the shift away from gasoline at the worst moment, with oil prices rising because of the war in Iran. They also note the promised $1,300 saving is not guaranteed to reach buyers, while fuel costs over a vehicle's life rise by about $1,600 on average — so many households could end up paying more overall, not less.

Fuel economy standards have swung back and forth with each administration since the 1970s, so the deeper story here is uncertainty: carmakers must design vehicles years in advance for rules that may be rewritten again. That instability has its own costs, pushing companies to hedge rather than commit fully to one technology.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: the EV market and California
perspectives.description: The article says the EV market's future depends heavily on the 2028 elections, meaning today's rollback may not last. Meanwhile California keeps its special right to require electric cars, so the real fight may move to Congress and the courts — and to whether other states follow California's stricter path.
